faq.a: Use a structured interview, ask about pill appearance, and involve family or caregivers. If still unclear, start with a broad safety net and monitor closely.
faq.q: What if the patient cannot recall all medications?

faq.a: Document the herb, review known interactions, and consider consulting a pharmacist or infectious disease specialist. If risk is high, adjust the antiretroviral regimen.
faq.q: How to handle a patient on an herbal remedy that may interact with antiretrovirals?

faq.a: Yes, rely on patient interview, pill counts, and any available prescriptions. Document the source and note any uncertainties.
faq.q: Can medication reconciliation be done without a pharmacy record?

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV patient on tenofovir/emtricitabine presents with new nausea. What is the first step in medication reconciliation? — Identify all current drugs, verify with pharmacy, and assess for drug‑induced nausea.

During a transfer from ward to ICU, a patient’s medication list is missing a recent dose of amlodipine. What is the most appropriate action? — Verify with the patient and pharmacy, correct the chart, and notify the ICU team.
A patient on antimalarial therapy reports taking an herbal tea daily. What should you consider? — Review potential interactions with artemisinin, document the herb, and monitor for toxicity.

A patient on warfarin develops a rash. How does medication reconciliation help? — Confirm all drugs, check for new OTC or herbal products that may increase bleeding risk, and adjust warfarin dose or switch therapy.

When a patient is discharged with a new medication but the pharmacy record shows no prior prescription, what is the next step? — Verify the prescription source, obtain a copy, and document the new drug in the discharge summary.
ai.title: Medication Reconciliation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A systematic process to verify a patient’s medications at every transition of care, preventing errors, adverse drug events, and ensuring continuity, especially critical in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Medication reconciliation is the structured collection, verification, and documentation of all drugs a patient takes, including prescription, OTC, herbal, and supplements, at every point of care change.

b: Use of pill counts when possible
Documentation in EMR or paper chart
sections.p: The core steps are: 1) Obtain a complete medication list from the patient and caregivers; 2) Verify against pharmacy records and prior charts; 3) Identify discrepancies; 4) Resolve and document changes; 5) Communicate updates to all providers.

t.b: If count < expected, ask about missed doses or hidden meds
If pharmacy record lacks a drug listed by patient, investigate source

b: Herbal products can potentiate or inhibit standard drugs
sections.p: In East African hospitals, common issues include herbal remedies, incomplete records, and limited lab access. Accurate reconciliation prevents interactions with antimalarials, antiretrovirals, and TB drugs.

b: Highlight importance of follow‑up after discharge
sections.p: Examiners often ask how you would handle a discrepancy or a patient on an unknown herbal supplement. Focus on systematic steps, patient communication, and documentation.

b: Not updating the chart after medication changes
sections.p: Assuming patient’s self‑reported list is complete, overlooking OTC and herbal drugs, failing to document changes, and not re‑checking at each transition.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe drug reaction (anaphylaxis, Stevens‑Johnson syndrome), unexplained hypotension, or new onset confusion after medication change
